b: GENERATES new content; discriminative models CLASSIFY input instead (benign/malicious)
Defense: phishing simulation, synthetic training data, automated report writing
Offense: phishing drafts, malware variants, deepfake content
Learns the data distribution, then produces similar-but-new samples
cards.tip: "Is it creating new content?" -> Generative. "Is it assigning a label/score?" -> Discriminative.

b: ML: learns patterns from data to make predictions without explicit programming (spam, malware detection)
Statistical learning: inference via statistical methods — anomaly detection, risk scoring
Statistical learning is the mathematical backbone of ML and is MORE EXPLAINABLE
cards.tip: If the scenario stresses "explainability," think statistical learning.

b: Deep learning: multi-layer neural nets for complex patterns (zero-day, deepfake detection)
It extracts features ITSELF rather than having them hand-engineered
Transformer: processes context IN PARALLEL via attention — the core architecture of LLMs
Difference from RNNs: parallel, not sequential -> training at massive scale becomes possible
cards.tip: "What architecture sits under LLMs?" -> Transformer.

b: Processes and understands human language: phishing-text analysis, threat-intel summarization
Turns UNSTRUCTURED text (logs, emails) into something processable
LLMs, SLMs, and chatbots are all applications within the NLP family
cards.tip: If the scenario mentions "text/language analysis," the family is NLP.

b: LLM: billions of parameters, general-purpose, cloud/GPU clusters, higher latency
SLM: few parameters, narrow task, runs LOCALLY on edge/single GPU, low latency
Air-gapped / OT-ICS / privacy scenario -> SLM (data never LEAVES the org)
SLM examples: Phi-3, Gemma, Mistral 7B
cards.tip: The moment you see "data can't go to the cloud / closed network," the answer is SLM.

cards.g: A duo that learns by competing
b: Generator vs. Discriminator: two networks learn by competing AGAINST each other
Result: highly realistic synthetic data
Offense: deepfake generation | Defense: synthetic training data, attack simulation
Exam trap: a GAN is NOT only an attack tool
cards.tip: When you see "two networks compete against each other" -> GAN.

b: Supervised: LABELED data -> classifying known threats (spam, malware signatures)
Unsupervised: UNLABELED data -> discovering unknown threats/anomalies (zero-day, UEBA)
Reinforcement: reward/penalty signal -> adaptive defense, response optimization
Zero-day scenario = no labels -> unsupervised anomaly detection
cards.tip: "Known or unknown?" decides it: known->supervised, unknown->unsupervised.

b: Checks performance on data the model HASN'T SEEN (the validation set)
Catches overfitting: exposes a model that shines in training but flops on real data
Cross-validation: splitting data into folds for a more reliable measure
The validation set tunes hyperparameters; the test set is saved for last
cards.tip: Don't mix up the roles of train / validation / test.

b: Fine-tuning: specializing a general model on domain-specific data
Epoch: one full pass over the training set; too many epochs = overfitting risk
Pruning: CUTS unnecessary connections -> structural shrinking
Quantization: LOWERS numeric precision (FP32->INT8) -> edge deployment
cards.tip: Pruning = structure changes, Quantization = precision changes. Both shrink; different mechanism.

cards.g: Data stays put, the model is shared
b: Training happens AT THE DATA OWNER; only model updates go to the center
Raw data is never shared -> privacy advantage (hospitals, banks, multi-branch)
Its risk: model poisoning — a malicious participant can send a tainted update
cards.tip: "Data can't be shared but we need a common model" -> Federated learning.

b: Zero-shot: 0 examples — fastest and cheapest, low-to-medium accuracy
One-shot: 1 example — ideal for demonstrating format
Multi-shot (few-shot): 2+ examples — most consistent output, highest accuracy and cost
As example count rises: accuracy up, token cost up
cards.tip: "No examples, need speed" -> zero-shot; "consistent format required, examples available" -> multi-shot.

b: System prompt: the model's identity and rules; usually HIDDEN from the user
User prompt: the user's actual request
System role: assigning a persona ("you are a SOC analyst") -> shapes the output
Template: a standard prompt skeleton -> consistency + a smaller injection surface
cards.tip: Hijacking the system prompt is the prime target of prompt injection.

b: Cleansing: removing errors/noise/duplicates -> catches poisoned samples early
Verification: checking accuracy and labels -> detects manipulation
Both are part of the data-prep pipeline; order: clean first, then verify
cards.tip: Cleansing = FIXES quality, Verification = CHECKS correctness.

b: Provenance = ORIGIN: where did the data come FROM? (source documentation)
Lineage = JOURNEY: what transformations did the data GO THROUGH? (end-to-end trail)
In incident response: provenance shows the poisoned data's source, lineage shows its spread
cards.tip: "From where?" -> Provenance, "through what?" -> Lineage. The exam makes you choose between these two.

b: The guarantee that data hasn't been corrupted or altered
Controls: hashing, digital signatures, checksums, audit logs
If training-data integrity breaks -> the door to data poisoning opens
cards.tip: "Tamper detection" = an integrity control (hash / signature).

b: Augmentation: growing the dataset with synthetic samples (for rare attack examples)
Balancing: fixing class imbalance -> raises recall in attack detection
Oversampling risk: OVERFITTING | Undersampling risk: INFORMATION LOSS
cards.tip: Grow the minority -> oversampling/overfitting; trim the majority -> undersampling/information loss.

b: Structured: fixed schema (SQL table, CSV) — high AI compatibility
Semi-structured: flexible schema (JSON, XML) — exam trap: JSON is NOT structured
Unstructured: schema-less (email, PDF, video) — ~80-90% of volume, needs preprocessing
cards.tip: JSON and XML are always SEMI-structured.

b: Embedding a hidden mark into AI-generated content -> proof of origin and ownership
Content watermarking: text / image / audio / video
Model watermarking: the MODEL ITSELF is marked -> evidence against model theft
A tracing tool for deepfake detection and IP protection
cards.tip: "Prove a stolen model" -> model watermarking; "identify AI content" -> content watermarking.

b: Flow: Query -> Embedding -> Vector search -> Relevant document -> LLM answer
Embeddings are NOT anonymous — an inversion attack can leak the original data
Vector storage risks: poisoning, unauthorized access
RAG REDUCES hallucination, it doesn't ELIMINATE it — the model can still misread context
cards.tip: "RAG ends hallucination" = wrong option. Treat embeddings like sensitive data.

b: The FIRST stage of the AI lifecycle: problem definition + alignment with org goals
Shift-left security: risk assessment and compliance checks START HERE
AI misaligned with goals = wasted resources + unmanaged risk
cards.tip: "At what stage should security begin?" -> at the very start, the business use case.

b: Trustworthiness: is the source RELIABLE? (general trust, reputation)
Authenticity: did the data really come FROM THAT SOURCE? (origin verification, signatures)
The two core security questions of the data-collection stage — related but DIFFERENT
cards.tip: Trust = trustworthiness, proof of origin = authenticity.

b: Data preparation: cleaning + labeling — manipulation and mislabeling risk
Model development/selection: off-the-shelf model risk -> AI supply chain, backdoors
Model evaluation: testing BEFORE deployment — performance + red team + bias review
cards.tip: Verifying the source when pulling a pre-built model = an AI supply-chain defense.

b: Deployment: hardening, API security, access control
Validation: real-world verification AFTER deployment (A/B, canary, shadow mode)
Monitoring: drift + attack detection, CONTINUOUS | Feedback: improvement — poisoning risk!
EVALUATION != VALIDATION: evaluation is pre-deploy, validation is post-deploy
cards.tip: Classic exam item: evaluation = test environment / BEFORE, validation = live / AFTER.

b: Human-in-the-loop: human approval AT THE MOMENT OF DECISION (for critical actions)
Human oversight: CONTINUOUS general monitoring (dashboards, audits) + kill switch
Human validation: expert review AFTER OUTPUT
The EU AI Act requires human oversight and an emergency stop for high-risk systems
cards.tip: Moment of decision -> HITL, continuous watching -> oversight, output check -> validation.

b: LLM-based application -> OWASP LLM Top 10
General ML model -> OWASP ML Security Top 10
Adversary tactics/techniques -> MITRE ATLAS (the AI version of ATT&CK)
Broad/ethical/social risk inventory -> MIT AI Risk Repository
Tracking a known AI flaw against a standard reference -> CVE AI Working Group
cards.tip: The keyword picks the source: "LLM app"->LLM Top10, "adversary technique"->ATLAS.

b: STRIDE: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, DoS, Elevation of privilege
MITRE ATLAS structure: Tactics (what they want) -> Techniques (how) -> Case Studies
Threat modeling = a continuous process, not a one-off
Defense in depth: a single control can be bypassed, layered controls hold
cards.tip: Know STRIDE's six letters cold; they may ask for each one's meaning in an AI context.

cards.g: Filter at the front, limit inside
b: Gateway controls: IN FRONT of the model, filter traffic (prompt firewall, rate/token limits)
Model controls: ON the model itself, constrain behavior (guardrails, evaluation)
Prompt firewall: blocks a malicious prompt BEFORE it reaches the model
Model guardrail: blocks harmful OUTPUT / masks sensitive info
cards.tip: On "where is it applied?": filtering->gateway, behavior->model.

b: Rate limit: requests per unit of TIME (defense against DoS, brute-force, scraping)
Token limit: tokens PER request (cost + context-overflow control)
Input quota: a ceiling on total SIZE (data size) and COUNT (quantity)
The three complement each other — one does NOT replace another
cards.tip: Requests/time->rate, tokens/request->token limit, total size->input quota. Don't mix them up.

b: Modality limits: TURN OFF unneeded modalities (a chatbot doesn't need image input? close it)
The simplest and most effective way to reduce attack surface
Guardrail testing & validation: NOT one-off, a CONTINUOUS process
Threats evolve -> guardrails must be retested continuously (red teaming)
cards.tip: "Disable the unneeded modality" is almost always the safest answer.

b: Model access has 4 tiers: inference (low risk) -> training/config/admin (high risk)
Data access: WRITE access to training data is the most critical (the poisoning door)
Agent access: an agent is AUTONOMOUS, it won't ask "does this make sense?" -> tightest control
Network/API access: authentication, IP whitelisting, API key rotation
cards.tip: Training access >> inference access in risk. Agent access should always be tighter.

b: Least privilege: applies to ALL FOUR access domains -> the universal correct answer
Network segmentation: training pipeline / inference API / DB on separate subnets
RAG metadata-based filtering: filter vector results by the user's permissions
API keys: keep them in a secret manager, never in code, rotate regularly
cards.tip: When unsure on an access question, least privilege is usually right.

b: In transit: moving over the network -> TLS/HTTPS (API calls)
At rest: sitting on disk -> AES (model files, databases)
In use: while being processed IN MEMORY -> confidential computing / TEE (still maturing)
Key management: even the strongest encryption fails if the key leaks -> HSM, KMS, rotation
cards.tip: "Protected even while processing" / "TEE" -> in-use encryption. Disk->rest, network->transit.

b: Anonymization: PERMANENT, irreversible, the person cannot be identified
Masking: format is PRESERVED, replaced with fake data, may be reversible
Redaction: information is BLACKED OUT/removed, format not preserved
Dynamic masking: on-the-fly, role-based (SOC sees differently) | Static: a permanent masked copy (test env)
cards.tip: Permanent+irreversible->anonymization, format kept+fake data->masking, black it out->redaction.

b: Classification: the foundation of ALL data-safety techniques — you can't protect what you haven't classified
Data minimization: DON'T COLLECT data you don't need -> a core GDPR principle
Classification labels determine the attack surface and compliance requirements
On compliance questions, "don't collect unnecessary data" is usually correct
cards.tip: "What do the other data-safety techniques rest on?" -> classification.

b: Monitoring: real-time, continuous, AUTOMATED
Auditing: periodic, in-depth, HUMAN-involved
Prompt monitoring: watches both the query (incoming) and the response (outgoing)
Rate monitoring != rate limiting: limiting BLOCKS, monitoring DETECTS (catches low-and-slow)
cards.tip: Monitoring detects, auditing reviews — one doesn't replace the other.

b: Log sanitization: scrub SENSITIVE INFO from logs (PII, prompt content, secrets)
Log protection: preserve log INTEGRITY — prevent tampering (WORM, signatures)
Different risks: sanitization for leakage, protection against deletion/alteration
Customer data in a model's response -> response monitoring + log sanitization
cards.tip: Sanitization = scrub the content, Protection = guard the log itself. Don't mix them.

b: Four cost dimensions: prompts (input tokens), storage (vectors/logs), response (output tokens), processing (compute)
A sudden cost spike -> could signal a DoS attack OR prompt flooding
Cost monitoring is both a FinOps and a SECURITY signal
Abnormal token consumption = an early warning of model DoS
cards.tip: On a "sudden cost spike" scenario, be able to name which dimension is affected.

b: Hallucination auditing: measure the made-up-output rate, add source verification
Accuracy: dropping accuracy = model drift OR adversarial input OR data quality
Bias auditing: disaggregated analysis — overall 95% may look fine while a subgroup sits at 70%
Access auditing: who accessed what? detecting unauthorized access
cards.tip: On bias, "disaggregated analysis": the overall average can hide bias, so measure subgroups separately.

b: Prompt injection: change the model's BEHAVIOR (LLM Top 10 #1, the most-asked)
Jailbreaking: remove the model's RESTRICTIONS — related but different
Evidence: instructions hidden via encoding, "ignore previous instructions" patterns
Control: prompt firewall + model guardrail + prompt templates (layered)
cards.tip: Injection=change behavior, Jailbreak=remove restrictions. Control: prompt FW + guardrail + template.

b: Data poisoning: manipulate the training DATA (mislabeling, injecting malicious samples)
Model poisoning: manipulate the MODEL ITSELF / its weights
Evidence: hash mismatch, unexpected model behavior, supply-chain breach
Control: data integrity controls + access controls + (for models) encryption
cards.tip: Data poisoning=data, model poisoning=weights. Both need data integrity + access control.

cards.g: Copy it vs. extract its data
b: Model theft: copy the model's BEHAVIOR via systematic queries (model extraction)
Model inversion: reconstruct the TRAINING DATA from outputs
Membership inference: determine WHETHER a record was in the training set
Common evidence: systematic/heavy querying | Common control: rate limiting + access control
cards.tip: Theft=copy behavior, Inversion=extract data, Membership=was the record in? All need rate limiting.

cards.g: Don't build on a base you don't trust
b: AI supply chain: a poisoned pre-trained model / library / dataset
Transfer learning attack: a poisoned base model stays malicious even after fine-tuning
Trojan/Backdoor: hidden malicious behavior triggered by a specific input
Control: model source verification + data integrity + access control + encryption
cards.tip: Verify the source of a downloaded model — that's the foundation of supply-chain defense.

b: Model skewing: manipulate the feedback loop to drift the model over time
Output integrity: alter the model's output after the fact (man-in-the-middle)
Input manipulation: trigger misclassification with adversarial input
Introducing biases: inject deliberate bias | Control: data integrity + guardrails
cards.tip: Skewing targets feedback, output integrity targets the output, input manipulation targets the input.

b: Excessive agency: an agent with more authority/autonomy than needed -> destructive actions
Insecure plug-in design: a plug-in with more access than it needs
Manipulating integrations: abusing connected systems (email, DB) through the AI
The shared fix for all three: LEAST PRIVILEGE + access controls
cards.tip: Any scenario where "the agent/plug-in is over-privileged" -> the answer is least privilege.

b: Model DoS: exhaust resources with expensive/complex queries (sponge attack)
Sensitive info disclosure: the model leaks sensitive info from training data
Insecure output handling: model output flows downstream unvalidated (XSS, SQLi)
DoS control: rate limit + prompt FW | Disclosure control: guardrails + encryption + access
cards.tip: Model DoS->rate limiting; sensitive disclosure->guardrails + output filtering.

cards.g: A process problem, not a technical one
b: Hallucination: the model produces confidently wrong/made-up output
Overreliance: users trusting AI output BLINDLY (not a technical attack)
Overreliance's fix isn't TECHNICAL but a PROCESS: human-in-the-loop, confidence warnings, training
Reducing hallucination: RAG, guardrails, prompt templates, source verification
cards.tip: Overreliance's fix isn't a technical control; it's HITL + confidence + awareness training.

b: IDE plug-in: the coding environment (risk: code leakage)
Browser plug-in: the web browser (risk: traffic monitoring)
CLI plug-in: the terminal | Chatbot: Q&A (risk: hallucination)
Personal assistant: a constant companion | MCP server: external-system integration
cards.tip: "MCP or chatbot?" type questions come up; know WHERE each tool runs.

cards.g: The connective tissue of agentic AI
b: MCP: an open standard for connecting an AI agent to external tools/services (USB-C-like)
Biggest risk: EXCESSIVE AGENCY / over-permissioning — the agent gets more authority than it needs
If the server is compromised, every connected service token (Gmail, Drive, etc.) is at risk
Fix: least privilege + tool filtering + continuous auditing (overlaps with OWASP LLM)
cards.tip: On an MCP question, the biggest risk is excessive agency; the fix is least privilege + tool filtering.

b: Signature matching: a KNOWN threat signature (classic AV/IDS logic)
Pattern recognition: a RECURRING structure (a known APT attack pattern)
Anomaly detection: DEVIATION from normal (something never seen / zero-day)
Known->signature/pattern, unknown->anomaly
cards.tip: "Never-seen attack"->anomaly; "known APT pattern"->pattern; "signature"->signature.

b: Reduce alert load / triage -> Incident management
Scan for known vulnerabilities -> Vulnerability analysis
Autonomous attack simulation -> Automated penetration testing
Code quality/bugs -> Code quality & linting | Fraud -> Fraud detection
cards.tip: Several options may be partly right; the question wants the MOST DIRECT solution.

b: Threat modeling: AI helps generate scenarios / attack trees
Translation: analyzing multilingual threat intel / phishing
Summarization: condensing long reports/logs/CTI -> saves the analyst time
These use cases bring AI's NLP power to defense
cards.tip: Summarization shortens a single source; synthesis (3.3) combines multiple sources.

b: Deepfakes aren't just video: voice cloning, face swaps, writing-style mimicry
Impersonation: "a fake call in the CEO's voice" -> deepfake impersonation
Misinformation = UNINTENTIONALLY false | Disinformation = DELIBERATELY false (only difference: intent)
In CEO fraud / BEC attacks, deepfake voice + text are used together
cards.tip: Mis vs. Dis is about INTENT. A deepfake voice is still a deepfake, not just video.

cards.g: A new attack, or a stronger one?
b: ENABLE: a new attack that couldn't exist without AI -> deepfakes, adversarial networks
ENHANCE: makes a traditional attack stronger -> phishing, DDoS, reconnaissance
Adversarial networks: using GANs to generate realistic fakes / evasion samples
Social engineering: AI's contribution is PERSONALIZATION + SCALE (success 2%->20%)
cards.tip: Deepfake/adversarial = ENABLE (new). Phishing/DDoS/recon = ENHANCE (made stronger).

b: Five sub-areas: attack vector discovery, payloads, malware, honeypot evasion, DDoS
Obfuscation: "polymorphic malware" -> every copy a different hash, same job (AI-assisted)
Automated data correlation: stitching scattered data into a target profile
AI SCALES and AUTOMATES the attack -> faster, cheaper, more of it
cards.tip: When you see "polymorphic malware" -> AI-assisted obfuscation.

b: Low-code: minimal coding knowledge, more FLEXIBLE | No-code: zero code, more LIMITED
"Automation without knowing how to code" -> No-code
Document synthesis: combine MULTIPLE sources into a NEW document
Summarization: condense a SINGLE document (don't confuse it with synthesis)
cards.tip: A non-coding manager -> no-code. Synthesis=combine+create, summarization=condense.

b: Code scanning (SAST) + Software composition analysis (dependencies/CVEs)
Unit testing + Regression testing (did old behavior break?)
Model testing: performance + adversarial + bias tests on every model update
Automated deployment/rollback: if a regression appears, deploy is BLOCKED
cards.tip: On every model update: performance+adversarial+bias tests; regression->block deploy.

b: AI agent weakness: missing the BIG PICTURE — isolated analysis (1 alert low, 50 alerts an attack)
AI's role in change mgmt: not to MAKE the decision, but to SUPPORT decision-making
Low-risk change -> AI auto-approve | High-risk -> human/CAB decision
AI-assisted approval + automated deployment/rollback speeds change up
cards.tip: AI doesn't approve a high-risk change on its own; CAB/human decision is required.

b: Ticket enrichment: AI automatically enriches the ticket with extra context
What it adds: IP reputation, past incidents, threat intel -> shortens investigation time
Triage: AI prioritizes alerts and filters false positives
The human analyst stays the final decision-maker (human-in-the-loop)
cards.tip: Ticket "enrichment" = AI auto-adding context/threat intel.

cards.g: Set the standard, delegate the work
b: AI Center of Excellence: sets standards, coordinates, oversees — doesn't run every project itself
Federated model: business units run projects, the CoE provides the standard
Policy = "WHAT must be done" (strategic rule) | Procedure = "HOW to do it" (step by step)
Main governance tools for shadow AI: an AI CoE + an Acceptable Use Policy
cards.tip: "Must pass a security test"->policy. "Step 1, Step 2..."->procedure. The CoE doesn't do every job itself.

b: Data Scientist (science/model development) vs. ML Engineer (engineering/production code)
ML Engineer (model code) vs. MLOps Engineer (operational automation, drift detection)
AI Architect (overall architecture) vs. AI Security Architect (security architecture)
Drift->MLOps | Risk assessment->Risk Analyst | Bias audit->Auditor | Policy enforcement->Governance Engineer
cards.tip: "Which role in this case?" comes up; know each role's one-sentence definition.

b: AI Governance Engineer: technically enforces policy/standard implementation
AI Risk Analyst: risk identification, assessment, prioritization
AI Auditor: must be INDEPENDENT — not involved in the system they audit (separation of duties)
Auditor + Risk Analyst + Governance Engineer = the GRC triangle
cards.tip: An AI Auditor must NOT be in the development/operation of the system they audit (independence).

b: Transparency: "HOW does the AI work?" — general openness (model cards, documentation)
Explainability: "WHY did the AI make this decision?" — specific decision rationale (SHAP, LIME)
Answer according to which question the scenario is asking
Both are Responsible AI principles but answer different questions
cards.tip: "How does it work"->transparency, "why this decision"->explainability. The most-asked distinction.

b: Fairness: decisions being FAIR (output) — "the model discriminates"
Inclusiveness: everyone being able to ACCESS it (input/access) — "the model can't serve some people"
Proxy variable: a variable correlated with a protected attribute (zip code/name/school) -> indirect bias
CompTIA classic: "loan agent unfairly approves a certain group" -> Introduction of bias
cards.tip: Fairness=output fairness, Inclusiveness=access. A proxy variable creates indirect bias.

b: Reliability & safety: consistent, safe operation | Privacy & security: data protection
Accountability: clear responsibility | Consistency: same input, same output
Awareness training: employees' awareness of AI risks
Differential privacy: individual records hidden while aggregate analysis stays possible (mathematical privacy)
cards.tip: Know each of the 9 principles in one sentence; "which principle is violated?" comes up.

b: Shadow AI: employees using UNAUTHORIZED AI tools -> a serious governance risk
Most effective fix: NOT an outright ban -> a safe alternative + policy + training
Autonomous systems risk: uncontrolled autonomous action -> human-in-the-loop + KILL SWITCH
Accidental data leakage: an employee pastes sensitive data into a public model
cards.tip: Shadow AI's fix isn't a ban; offer a safe alternative. Autonomous risk->HITL + kill switch.

b: IP-related risk: training on copyrighted data, unclear ownership of model output
Reputational loss: bias/hallucination/leakage going public -> brand damage
Accuracy & performance: the model decays over time (drift) -> wrong decisions
These risks are managed at the BUSINESS/GRC level, not the technical one
cards.tip: IP, reputation, accuracy = business-level risks; the fix is governance + monitoring + policy.

b: 4 risk tiers: Unacceptable (banned) > High > Limited (transparency) > Minimal
High-risk examples: employment, education, credit scoring, law enforcement, medical
Chatbot->Limited (transparency) | Spam filter->Minimal
Fine: 35M EUR OR 7% of global turnover — even higher than GDPR
cards.tip: Employment/credit/law-enforcement->High risk. Fine 35M EUR / 7%. Most-asked: "which risk category?"

cards.g: Law vs. Principles vs. Standard vs. Framework
b: EU AI Act: a LEGAL REQUIREMENT (law)
OECD: international PRINCIPLES (non-binding)
ISO/IEC 42001: a technical STANDARD + certification (the AI version of ISO 27001)
NIST AI RMF: a risk-management FRAMEWORK — 4 functions: Govern, Map, Measure, Manage
cards.tip: Legal->EU AI Act, principles->OECD, standard/certification->ISO 42001, risk framework->NIST RMF.

b: Data sovereignty: the PHYSICAL location of data + which country's law applies
In cloud AI, the data-center region is a critical compliance concern
Sanctioned vs. unsanctioned: approved/unapproved tool use (ties to shadow AI)
Sensitive data (health/defense/finance) -> private model or hybrid; general use -> public is fine
cards.tip: Sensitive data->private/hybrid model. Data sovereignty=data location + applicable law.

cards.g: How do you vet a provider?
b: Evaluation elements: SOC 2, ISO 27001, DPA (Data Processing Agreement)
SLA + data-center location + sub-processor chain
"How do you assess the provider?" -> answer with these elements
Third-party compliance = part of AI supply-chain governance
cards.tip: Provider evaluation: SOC 2 + ISO 27001 + DPA + SLA + data-center location.
